cultivar: Yunnan large-leaf (Camellia sinensis var. assamica), bud-rich spring plantation and arbor leaf
processing: Sun-dried maocha is wet-piled to full fermentation, then the finest fraction, tiny buds and bud-leaves that turn golden in the pile, is sieved out as the top grade; sold loose or pressed into small cakes and bricks.
harvest_season: Sorted from piles made of spring and autumn maocha; sold by production year rather than by harvest.
appearance_dry: Very small, tight, dark leaves thick with golden-brown buds, almost like fine black tea; pressed versions have a solid gold face.
appearance_liquor: Dark, glossy red-brown, very clear, with a thick look and a bright ring at the edge of the cup.
appearance_wet: A fine, even mass of small brown buds and leaf tips.
taste_profile: Rich and dense: a fragrant, slightly sweet aroma of dates and cocoa, a thick creamy body, a hint of bitterness from the buds, a clean earthiness and a long smooth finish; intense early and spent sooner than coarser grades.

brewing.notes: Rinse twice, fast, with boiling water; fine buds give up colour instantly, so keep the first steeps to a few seconds. Use a strainer. Expect a strong first half and a quick fade after six or seven steeps.

vintage_note: Sold by production year, loose by weight or as small pressed cakes, bricks and dragon balls, and the grade name appeared in the Menghai trade only in the late 1990s, so there is no gong ting older than that. It is bought young to mid-aged (1–8 years) for its richness and aroma; the fine bud material loses its pile smell quickly, drinks well within a year, and does not gain much beyond about ten years, so very old gong ting is unusual and expensive without being obviously better. 'Palace grade' is a sieve grade, not a quality guarantee, and the price should track the cleanliness of the fermentation rather than the romance of the name.
description:
Gong ting, 'palace grade', is the finest sieve grade of ripe pu-erh: the tiny buds and bud-leaves that come out of the fermentation pile golden-brown and are separated from the coarser leaf. The name is pure marketing from the late 1990s, nodding at Qing tribute tea, but the grade is real and it makes a distinctive cup, dense, fragrant and creamy.

The material is ordinary wet-piled shu; what differs is the sorting. After fermentation and drying the tea is sieved, and the smallest fraction is sold separately, loose or pressed into small cakes, bricks and dragon balls. Because buds carry more caffeine and more of the compounds that give aroma, gong ting is more intense than a grade-7 cake and also gives out faster.

In the cup it is thick and glossy, dark red-brown, with dates, cocoa and a faintly sweet fragrance, a creamy texture, a whisper of bud bitterness and a clean earthiness; the first five steeps are excellent and the tea is largely spent by eight. Flash the early infusions, because the fine leaf colours water instantly, and use a strainer. It is a tea for a short, rich session rather than a long afternoon.

It is sold by production year, usually at a premium over ordinary grades, loose by weight from the bigger factories and as pressed pieces from boutique makers. The grade says nothing about where the leaf came from or how cleanly it was fermented, so judge on the nose: a clean date-and-cocoa aroma is right, any sourness or fishiness is a fermentation fault at any price. Jin Ya (golden bud) tea is the same idea described by its looks.

It makes a luxurious winter breakfast tea and takes milk better than most pu-erh, if that is your thing.
sources_note: The late-1990s appearance of the 'gong ting' grade name is from Menghai trade history (often tied to the Menghai Tea Factory around 1999); the exact year varies by source.
